unit_label: CB Module F unit 1: non-banking financial institutions, development, regulation and supervision (courseware unit 17)

facts.statement: NBFC registration and types (courseware): banks mobilise deposits from the public and finance activities through lending; unlike banks, NBFCs are not governed by the Banking Regulation Act and receive money as a whole or in instalments connected with a scheme; conditions to register with the Reserve Bank as an NBFC: the business must be registered as a company under the Companies Act, 1956 or 2013; the minimum capital (Net Owned Fund) requirement is Rs 2 crore; the principal business must be financial activities (if the financial flow of the business is more than 50 per cent of total capital asset, the company can get NBFC registration); there should be at least one Director from the financial field or a senior banker as a director; and the CIBIL records should be clean; companies may be registered as deposit accepting or non-deposit accepting NBFCs (ND is suffixed to the name); NBFCs with an asset size of Rs 100 crore or more are known as Systemically Important NBFCs (NBFC-SI); the non-deposit accepting systemically important NBFCs are known as NBFC-NDSI; some NBFCs are regulated by other bodies: insurance companies by IRDA, housing finance companies by the National Housing Bank, stock-broking companies, merchant banking companies, mutual funds, venture capital companies and companies running collective investment schemes by SEBI, chit fund companies under the Chit Fund Act and the State Governments, and Nidhi companies by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs.
facts.locator: S05 courseware unit 17, printed pp. 436-437 (PDF pp. 453-454), sections 17.1 to 17.3

facts.statement: Classification of NBFCs by activity (courseware Table 17.1, 11 categories): Investment and Credit Company (ICC) for lending and investment; NBFC-Infrastructure Finance Company (NBFC-IFC) for financing the infrastructure sector; Core Investment Company (CIC) for investment in equity shares, preference shares, debt or loans of group companies; NBFC-Infrastructure Debt Fund (NBFC-IDF) to facilitate the flow of long-term debt into post-commencement operations infrastructure projects that have completed at least one year of satisfactory performance; NBFC-Micro Finance Institution (NBFC-MFI) providing collateral free small ticket loans to economically disadvantaged groups; NBFC-Factor for acquiring receivables of an assignor or extending loans against the security interest of the receivables at a discount; NBFC-Non-Operative Financial Holding Company (NBFC-NOFHC) to facilitate promoters or promoter groups in setting up new banks; Mortgage Guarantee Company (MGC) for undertaking mortgage guarantee business; NBFC-Account Aggregator (NBFC-AA) collecting and providing information about a customer financial assets in a consolidated, organised and retrievable manner to the customer or others as specified by the customer; NBFC-Peer to Peer Lending Platform (NBFC-P2P) providing an online platform to bring lenders and borrowers together to help mobilise funds; and Housing Finance Company (HFC) financing housing.
facts.locator: S05 courseware unit 17, printed pp. 437-438 (PDF pp. 454-455), section 17.4 Table 17.1

facts.statement: Growth and RBI role (courseware): between March 31, 2009 and March 31, 2019 the total assets of NBFCs grew at a compounded annual growth rate (CAGR) of 18.6 per cent, while the balance sheets of scheduled commercial banks grew at a CAGR of 10.7 per cent; NBFCs have become the largest net borrowers of funds from the financial system, with more than half of the funds from SCBs, followed by asset management companies-mutual funds and insurance companies; the Reserve Bank is entrusted with the regulation and supervision of NBFCs under the provisions contained in Chapter III B and C and Chapter V of the RBI Act, 1934; the framework covers registration of NBFCs, prudential regulation, directions on acceptance of deposits and surveillance through off-site and on-site supervision, with deposit taking NBFCs and Systemically Important Non-Deposit Accepting companies subject to a greater degree of regulation; the focus of regulation and supervision is three-fold: depositor protection, consumer protection and financial stability; the Reserve Bank is empowered under the RBI Act to take punitive action including cancellation of the Certificate of Registration, orders of prohibition from accepting deposits, filing criminal cases, or winding up petitions; the Reserve Bank also co-ordinates with State Governments on legislation against unauthorised and fraudulent activities, conducts public awareness programmes, promotes a Self-Regulatory Organisation (SRO) for NBFC-MFI and trains personnel of NBFCs, State Governments, State Police and auditors.
facts.locator: S05 courseware unit 17, printed pp. 438-439 (PDF pp. 455-456), sections 17.5 and 17.6

facts.statement: Scale-based regulation and supervisory policies (courseware): the Reserve Bank released a scale-based regulation framework for NBFCs on October 22, 2021 with a four-layered structure: base layer (NBFC-BL), middle layer (NBFC-ML), upper layer (NBFC-UL) and a top layer; the base layer consists of non-deposit taking NBFCs with asset size below Rs 1,000 crore and certain other NBFCs engaged in specific activities; the middle layer mainly includes all deposit taking NBFCs and non-deposit taking NBFCs with asset size of Rs 1,000 crore and above and some specialised NBFCs; the upper layer comprises certain NBFCs specifically identified by the Reserve Bank on the basis of a set of parameters and scoring methodology and will be subject to enhanced regulatory rigour; the top layer is proposed to remain empty unless the Reserve Bank takes a view that a specific NBFC in the upper layer poses systemic risk; the framework is effective from October 01, 2022; the Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP) is to be made proportionate to the scale and complexity of operations; the capital to risk weighted assets ratio (CRAR) requirement for NBFCs is 15 per cent of risk weighted assets; NBFC-UL must maintain a Common Equity Tier 1 capital of at least 9 per cent of RWAs; large exposure norms apply to NBFC-UL with a limit of 25 per cent for a single borrower and 40 per cent for a group of borrowers in case of NBFC-ML and NBFC-UL; the NPA classification was changed to the overdue period of more than 90 days for all categories of NBFCs; NBFC-UL and NBFC-ML must put in place a Board approved policy and a Compliance Function with the appointment of a Chief Compliance Officer (CCO); the Reserve Bank issued guidelines in April 2021 for the appointment of Statutory Central Auditors and Statutory Auditors of SCBs (excluding RRBs), UCBs and NBFCs including HFCs; the Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework for NBFCs was put in place in December 2021 and is effective from October 1, 2022 based on the financials at end-March 2022, applicable to all deposit taking NBFCs (excluding government NBFCs) and all non-deposit taking NBFCs in the middle, upper and top layers (excluding NBFCs not accepting public funds, government companies and primary dealers); for NBFCs-D and NBFCs-ND (excluding core investment companies) the key monitoring parameters are capital (CRAR and Tier I capital ratio) and asset quality (net NPA ratio), and for CICs leverage is an additional parameter; the regulation of HFCs was transferred from the National Housing Bank to the Reserve Bank with effect from August 9, 2019, and the net owned fund requirement for HFCs was increased from Rs 10 crore to Rs 20 crore; guidelines on dividend declaration by NBFCs were issued on June 24, 2021.
facts.locator: S05 courseware unit 17, printed pp. 439-443 (PDF pp. 456-460), sections 17.7 to 17.15

payload.title: Registering an NBFC and the types of NBFC
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Conditions:** a **company** under the Companies Act; **Net Owned Fund Rs 2 crore**; **principal business financial**; at least one **director from the financial field**; **clean CIBIL records**.

**Types:** deposit accepting or **ND**; **NBFC-SI** (asset size Rs 100 crore or more); **NBFC-NDSI** are the non-deposit accepting systemically important ones.

**Other regulators:** **IRDA** (insurance), **NHB** (housing finance, in the courseware text), **SEBI** (brokers, merchant banks, mutual funds, venture capital, CIS), **State Governments** (chit funds), **MCA** (Nidhi).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Unlike banks, NBFCs are not governed by the Banking Regulation Act. A company outside the Reserve Bank's registration is regulated by the body that governs its activity.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the minimum Net Owned Fund for NBFC registration, as stated in this unit?

payload.title: The 11 NBFC categories by activity
payload.core_explanation_md: **ICC** (lending and investment); **IFC** (infrastructure finance); **CIC** (group company holdings); **IDF** (long-term debt into mature infrastructure projects, **one year of satisfactory performance**); **MFI** (collateral free small ticket loans); **Factor** (receivables); **NOFHC** (promoters setting up new banks); **MGC** (mortgage guarantee); **AA** (consolidated financial information to the customer); **P2P** (online lender-borrower platform); **HFC** (housing finance).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The categories are defined by activity, so one NBFC fits one category. Account aggregators move data, not funds.

self_check.prompt_text: Which NBFC category facilitates promoters in setting up new banks?

payload.title: Growth and the Reserve Bank role
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Growth:** NBFC assets grew at a **18.6 per cent CAGR** from March 2009 to March 2019 against **10.7 per cent** for scheduled commercial banks.

**Regulation:** under **Chapters III B, III C and V of the RBI Act, 1934**; **three-fold focus: depositor protection, consumer protection and financial stability**.

**Punitive powers:** **cancel the Certificate of Registration**, **prohibit deposit acceptance**, **criminal cases** or **winding up petitions**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The sector's interconnection with banks (most of its funds come from SCBs) is why stress can transmit between them. The RBI also promotes an SRO for NBFC-MFIs.

self_check.prompt_text: What are the three aims of NBFC regulation?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Depositor protection, consumer protection and financial stability.

payload.title: Scale-based regulation and supervisory policies
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Four layers:** **Base** (non-deposit taking, below Rs 1,000 crore), **Middle** (all deposit takers and Rs 1,000 crore and above), **Upper** (RBI-identified by parameters and scoring), **Top** (empty unless the RBI sees systemic risk); effective **1 October 2022**.

**Norms:** **CRAR 15 per cent**; **CET1 at least 9 per cent** for the upper layer; **single/group borrower exposure 25 / 40 per cent**; **NPA at more than 90 days overdue**; **Chief Compliance Officer** for upper and middle layers.

**PCA:** from **1 October 2022**; key parameters **CRAR, Tier I and net NPA**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The scale-based approach lets regulation grow with size and risk. HFCs came under the Reserve Bank from 9 August 2019.

self_check.prompt_text: Which layer is proposed to remain empty unless the RBI sees systemic risk?

payload.stem_md: An NBFC has risk weighted assets of Rs 800 crore and must hold CRAR of 15 per cent. What minimum capital must it hold, in crore rupees?
An NBFC-UL has RWA of Rs 2,000 crore and must hold CET1 of 9 per cent. What is the minimum CET1, in crore rupees?
An NBFC-ML has Tier 1 capital of Rs 400 crore. What is the single borrower exposure limit at 25 per cent, in crore rupees?
An NBFC-ML has Tier 1 capital of Rs 400 crore. What is the group of borrowers exposure limit at 40 per cent, in crore rupees?
An NBFC sector has assets of Rs 100 lakh crore growing at 18.6 per cent for one year. What are the assets after one year, in lakh crore rupees?
The growth rate of NBFCs was 18.6 per cent and of SCBs 10.7 per cent. What is the difference, in percentage points?
A company has a financial flow of Rs 60 crore against total capital assets of Rs 100 crore. What is the financial flow as a percentage, in per cent?
payload.correct_explanation_md: 60 / 100 = 60 per cent, above the 50 per cent test.

No primary source (RBI master directions, circulars) was retrieved; thresholds and dates are taught only as the courseware states them and may have changed by the 30 June 2026 cut-off.

Held back as dated and not asked in any question: the asset size of the NBFC sector (Rs 51.47 lakh crore as at March 2020), the 2020 Special Liquidity Scheme amount (Rs 30,000 crore) and its disbursement (Rs 7,126 crore, 53 per cent to NBFCs), the SARFAESI thresholds (Rs 100 crore asset size, Rs 50 lakh and Rs 20 lakh debt) and the pandemic GDP contraction in the first quarter of 2020-21.

The courseware states that NBFCs with asset size of Rs 100 crore or more are Systemically Important NBFCs (NBFC-SI) in the registration section, while the scale-based framework (October 22, 2021) uses Rs 1,000 crore as the base-layer boundary; both are taught as stated, as separate regimes, and flagged as dated.
The courseware says the Financial flow of the business must be more than 50 per cent of total capital assets for NBFC registration; the exact twin tests (principal business) are taught as stated.

The courseware text on the CRAR for NBFCs-ND says 15 per cent (consistent with the key) and says the base layer NBFCs-BL and middle layer follow it; the upper layer has Common Equity Tier 1 of at least 9 per cent of RWA; taught as stated.
